questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Java's type system?

options.text: Statically and strongly typed; each variable and expression has a compile-time type
Dynamically typed; types are assigned only at runtime
Weakly typed; any value can be used with any operator
Untyped; types are documentation only

questions.explanation: The Java Language Specification describes Java as statically typed: every variable and expression has a type known at compile time, and that type restricts values and operations.

questions.prompt: Which list contains all eight Java primitive types?

options.text: boolean, byte, short, int, long, char, float, double
Boolean, Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Character, Float, Double
byte, short, int, long, String, float, double, char
boolean, byte, short, integer, long, char, decimal, double

questions.explanation: The primitive types are boolean and the numeric primitives byte, short, int, long, char, float, and double. Wrapper classes such as Integer are reference types, not primitives.

questions.prompt: Java's char type represents a 16-bit unsigned UTF-16 code unit, not necessarily a complete Unicode code point.
questions.explanation: The JLS defines char as a 16-bit unsigned integer representing a UTF-16 code unit. Some Unicode code points require a surrogate pair of two char values.

questions.prompt: An int multiplication that overflows automatically throws ArithmeticException.
questions.explanation: Ordinary integer arithmetic does not signal overflow; the result retains the low-order bits. Integer division or remainder by zero, unlike overflow, can throw ArithmeticException.

questions.prompt: What is the result type of `intValue + longValue` when `intValue` is int and `longValue` is long?

options.text: long, after the int operand is widened
int, after the long operand is narrowed
double
The operands must be explicitly cast or compilation fails

questions.explanation: Binary numeric promotion uses long precision when either integer operand is long; the int operand is widened to long first.

questions.prompt: Casting a double value to int rounds it to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: A floating-point-to-integral narrowing conversion truncates toward zero, subject to the specified range behavior; it does not round to nearest.

questions.prompt: Which claim about `==` on two object references is correct?

options.text: It tests whether the references identify the same object
It always calls the objects' equals method
It compares every field recursively
It is illegal for reference types

questions.explanation: Reference equality compares object identity. Value-based equality is defined by an appropriate equals implementation, where the class provides one.

questions.prompt: Java evaluates the operands of an operator from left to right.
questions.explanation: The JLS specifies left-to-right operand evaluation, including evaluating a method invocation's argument expressions from left to right.

questions.prompt: What does `&&` do that `&` does not when both operands are boolean?

options.text: && short-circuits: it skips the right operand when the left is false
&& evaluates both operands in parallel
& is not valid for boolean values
&& returns an integer bit mask

questions.explanation: Conditional-and `&&` evaluates the right operand only if the left operand is true. Boolean `&` evaluates both operands.

questions.prompt: The expression `0.0 / 0.0` with double operands produces NaN rather than ArithmeticException.
questions.explanation: Floating-point division follows IEEE 754 behavior and yields NaN for zero divided by zero. Integer division by zero instead throws ArithmeticException.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Java class inheritance is correct?

options.text: A class has at most one direct superclass, but can implement multiple interfaces
A class may extend any number of classes
A class cannot implement interfaces if it extends a class
Every class must explicitly extend Object

questions.explanation: A class extends one direct superclass and may implement multiple interfaces. A normal class without an extends clause has Object as its direct superclass, except Object itself.

questions.prompt: A Java abstract class can be instantiated directly with `new`.
questions.explanation: An abstract class cannot be instantiated. A concrete subclass can be instantiated if it implements inherited abstract methods.

questions.prompt: What does declaring a class `final` prevent?

options.text: It prevents the class from having subclasses
It prevents instances from being created
It makes every field deeply immutable
It makes all methods static

questions.explanation: A final class cannot be subclassed. The modifier does not by itself make its instances immutable or prevent instantiation.

questions.prompt: What is the principal role of a Java constructor?

options.text: Initialize a newly created class instance
Return an instance to the caller with a declared return type
Override a superclass method
Run once when the class is loaded

questions.explanation: Constructors initialize new instances and are invoked during instance creation. They have no return type and are not ordinary methods.

questions.prompt: A subclass constructor can call a superclass constructor using `super(...)` as its explicit constructor invocation.
questions.explanation: A constructor can explicitly invoke a superclass constructor using a superclass constructor invocation, subject to Java's constructor-body rules.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid purpose of an interface in Java?

options.text: Define a reference type and contract that classes can implement
Provide multiple class inheritance of instance state
Declare constructors for implementing classes
Store per-instance mutable fields for implementors

questions.explanation: An interface declares a reference type that classes can implement; its contract can include abstract, default, static, and other permitted members, but it is not a superclass with instance state.

questions.prompt: A concrete class that implements an interface must implement its abstract methods, unless it inherits suitable implementations.
questions.explanation: A non-abstract class must provide or inherit implementations for all abstract interface methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract.

questions.prompt: What is method overloading?

options.text: Declaring methods with the same name but different parameter signatures
Replacing an inherited method with a compatible implementation
Hiding a field with a local variable
Calling a method through a superclass reference

questions.explanation: Overloading provides multiple methods with the same name but distinct signatures, commonly different parameter lists. Overriding replaces an inherited instance-method implementation.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes overriding from static method hiding?

options.text: Overriding applies to instance methods and uses runtime dispatch; static methods are hidden, not overridden
Both are selected only from the runtime object's class
Static methods cannot be inherited
Overriding requires a different method name

questions.explanation: Instance method overriding participates in dynamic dispatch. A static method declaration with a matching signature hides an inherited static method; static selection is not polymorphic instance dispatch.

questions.prompt: A record class is implicitly final and cannot be directly subclassed by an ordinary class.
questions.explanation: Record classes are implicitly final. They provide a concise class form for a fixed set of component values.

questions.prompt: What does a sealed class declaration control?

options.text: Which classes may directly extend it
Which methods may be overloaded
Whether objects can be garbage-collected
Which packages may import it

questions.explanation: A sealed class restricts its permitted direct subclasses, using a permits clause or permitted subclasses inferred under the language rules.

questions.prompt: Which class member is shared at the class level rather than stored separately in each instance?

options.text: A static field
An instance field
A constructor parameter
A local variable in an instance method

questions.explanation: A static field is a class variable, with one incarnation associated with the class; an instance field is associated with each object instance.

questions.prompt: A static nested class has an immediately enclosing instance of its outer class, just like an inner class.
questions.explanation: A static nested class has no immediately enclosing instance. A non-static inner class instance is associated with an enclosing instance.

questions.prompt: Which annotation asks the compiler to verify that a method overrides an inherited method?

options.text: @Override
@Inherited
@FunctionalInterface
@SuppressWarnings

questions.explanation: @Override marks an intended override; the compiler reports an error if the declaration does not override a method as required by the language rules.

questions.prompt: An enum constant may have a class body that specializes behavior for that constant.
questions.explanation: Enum constants can have class bodies, creating constant-specific class implementations within the enum's permitted structure.

questions.prompt: Why can `List<String>` not be assigned to a variable of type `List<Object>`?

options.text: Generic types are invariant, so those parameterizations are distinct types
String is not a subtype of Object
List cannot contain reference types
The assignment requires a cast because all generic types are covariant

questions.explanation: Java generic classes are invariant: even though String is a subtype of Object, List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>. Wildcards express safe variance where needed.

questions.prompt: Which parameter type can accept a `List<Integer>` when a method only needs to read elements as numbers?

options.text: List<? extends Number>
List<Number> only
List<? super Integer> only
List<int>

questions.explanation: An upper-bounded wildcard accepts a list parameterized by Number or a subtype such as Integer and exposes elements as Number for reading. Primitive types cannot be generic arguments.

questions.prompt: For a consumer that inserts Integer values, which wildcard is generally suitable?

options.text: ? super Integer
? extends Integer
? extends Object only
? void

questions.explanation: A lower-bounded wildcard such as ? super Integer can represent a collection whose element type is Integer or a supertype, allowing Integer values to be added safely. This reflects the consumer-super principle.

questions.prompt: `List<?>` can be used to read elements as Object, but generally does not permit adding an arbitrary non-null value.
questions.explanation: The exact element type is unknown, so a value of an arbitrary type cannot be safely added. Reading yields Object; null is permitted because it is compatible with every reference type.

questions.prompt: Java generic type arguments such as String and Integer are fully retained as distinct parameterized runtime classes.
questions.explanation: Java uses type erasure for generic parameterized types: different parameterizations of a generic class share the same class at runtime, with some type information erased.

questions.prompt: Which is a reifiable type?

options.text: List<?>
List<String>
T where T is a type variable
List<? extends Number>

questions.explanation: A parameterized type whose arguments are all unbounded wildcards is reifiable. List<String> and bounded-wildcard parameterizations are not reifiable under the JLS definition.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a type parameter bound such as `<T extends Number>`?

options.text: Restrict T to types satisfying the stated upper bound and expose its members
Require T to be exactly Number
Make T a primitive type
Disable compile-time checking for T

questions.explanation: A bound constrains valid type arguments to subtypes of the bound and lets code use members available through the bound. `extends` is used for both class and interface bounds.

questions.prompt: A generic class may directly extend Throwable and use a type parameter to parameterize its exception type.
questions.explanation: The JLS forbids a generic class from being a direct or indirect subclass of Throwable; generic exception classes are not permitted.

questions.prompt: What does the diamond operator `new ArrayList<>()` primarily allow the compiler to do?

options.text: Infer constructor type arguments from the surrounding target type
Create a raw type with no generic checks
Make the collection immutable
Select a parallel collection implementation

questions.explanation: The diamond lets the compiler infer type arguments for a generic class instance creation expression from context rather than repeating them explicitly.

questions.prompt: A raw type such as `List` bypasses some generic type checking and can lead to unchecked warnings or heap pollution.
questions.explanation: Raw types exist primarily for compatibility with pre-generics code. Their use can bypass generic checks, producing unchecked operations and possible heap pollution.

questions.prompt: Which declaration is a generic method, rather than merely a method in a generic class?

options.text: `static <T> T identity(T value)`
`T get()` in `class Box<T>`
`String get()` in `class Box`
`void set(Object value)`

questions.explanation: A generic method declares its own type parameter section, here `<T>`, independently of whether its enclosing class is generic.

questions.prompt: The same generic class can have distinct runtime class identities for `Box<String>` and `Box<Integer>` solely because of their type arguments.
questions.explanation: Parameterized types share the same generic class at runtime under type erasure; type arguments do not create separate runtime classes.

questions.prompt: Why does `List<Integer>` not mean a list of primitive int values?

options.text: Generic type arguments must be reference types; use the wrapper Integer
Generics accept only interfaces
Integer is a primitive alias
List stores all values as strings

questions.explanation: Java type arguments are reference types or wildcards; primitive types cannot be type arguments. Wrapper types such as Integer enable collections of numeric values.

questions.prompt: What does type erasure do to a generic method's signature?

options.text: Maps parameterized types and type variables in the signature to non-parameterized erased types
Deletes the method body
Converts all arguments to strings
Makes generic method overloading depend on return type alone

questions.explanation: The JLS defines erasure for types and maps generic method/constructor signatures to signatures without parameterized types or type variables; this creates restrictions such as erasure clashes.

questions.prompt: A type variable with no explicit bound has Object as its implicit bound.
questions.explanation: If a type variable has no declared bound, the JLS assumes Object as its bound.

questions.prompt: Which types are unchecked exception classes in Java?

options.text: RuntimeException and its subclasses, plus Error and its subclasses
All subclasses of Exception
Only IOException
Throwable and every subclass

questions.explanation: The JLS defines unchecked exception classes as runtime exception classes (RuntimeException and subclasses) and error classes (Error and subclasses). Other exception classes are checked.

questions.prompt: A checked exception that a method can throw must be caught or declared in its throws clause.
questions.explanation: Compile-time checking requires a handler or a compatible throws declaration for checked exceptions that can result from a method or constructor body.

questions.prompt: What is the superclass relationship between Error and Exception?

options.text: Both are direct subclasses of Throwable and are siblings
Error extends Exception
Exception extends Error
Neither extends Throwable

questions.explanation: Throwable is the common superclass; Exception and Error are separate direct subclasses. RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception.

questions.prompt: What does `finally` normally provide in a try statement?

options.text: A block that executes as control leaves the try/catch, including during exception propagation
A guarantee that the process survives every fatal VM error
A replacement for checked-exception declarations
A block that runs only when no exception occurs

questions.explanation: A finally block is executed during normal or abrupt completion of the associated try/catch, subject to process termination and other exceptional circumstances. Abrupt completion of finally can override a prior reason for completion.

questions.prompt: `catch (Exception e)` also catches instances of Error because Error and Exception share Throwable as a superclass.
questions.explanation: A catch clause catches instances of its declared type or subclasses. Error is a sibling of Exception, so catching Exception does not catch Error.

questions.prompt: Why must catch clauses generally list a more specific exception before a broader superclass exception?

options.text: A preceding broad catch would make a later subtype catch unreachable
Java sorts catch clauses alphabetically
A subtype cannot be caught directly
Only one catch clause is allowed

questions.explanation: Catch clauses are examined in order; a later clause is a compile-time error if an earlier clause already catches that type or a superclass of it.

questions.prompt: A method overriding a method that declares checked exceptions may add any new checked exception to its throws clause.
questions.explanation: An overriding method's throws clause must be compatible with the overridden method and cannot add a checked exception that the overridden declaration does not permit.

questions.prompt: Which exception mechanism does try-with-resources use for resource cleanup?

options.text: It automatically invokes close on declared resources as the statement exits
It relies on garbage collection to close resources
It closes every object referenced inside the try block
It suppresses every exception from close

questions.explanation: Try-with-resources automatically closes declared resources that implement the relevant resource contract when the statement completes, including exceptional completion.

questions.prompt: The compiler generally requires checked exceptions to be declared or handled, but does not require RuntimeException subclasses to be declared.
questions.explanation: RuntimeException subclasses are unchecked and exempt from compile-time catch-or-declare checking; checked exceptions are subject to that requirement.

questions.prompt: What happens when a thrown exception reaches no matching handler in the current thread?

options.text: The current thread terminates after applicable finally blocks run
The JVM retries the throwing statement indefinitely
The exception is automatically converted to null
Every other thread must also terminate

questions.explanation: If no matching catch is found, the current thread terminates; finally clauses are executed during propagation, and uncaught-exception handling may then occur.

questions.prompt: Which Java SE API module contains foundational types such as those in `java.lang` and `java.util`?

options.text: java.base
java.sql
java.desktop
jdk.compiler

questions.explanation: The Java SE API specification identifies java.base as the module defining foundational Java SE APIs, including core language and utility packages.

questions.prompt: The List interface represents an ordered collection whose elements can be accessed by position.
questions.explanation: List is the ordered collection abstraction with positional access. Its concrete implementations differ in performance and mutability characteristics.

questions.prompt: Which Map implementation is generally chosen for expected constant-time lookup by key without sorted order?

options.text: HashMap
TreeMap
ArrayDeque
LinkedList

questions.explanation: HashMap is the hash-table Map implementation and provides expected constant-time basic operations when hashes disperse keys properly. TreeMap maintains sorted-key order with logarithmic operations.

questions.prompt: TreeMap maintains its entries according to key ordering rather than insertion order.
questions.explanation: TreeMap is a NavigableMap implementation ordered by natural key order or a supplied Comparator, not insertion order.

questions.prompt: What must generally be true when a class overrides `equals` for use as a HashMap key?

options.text: It must also implement a consistent hashCode so equal objects have equal hashes
hashCode must return a unique value for every object
equals must compare object identity only
The class must implement Comparable

questions.explanation: The Object contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes. Unequal objects may share a hash code, though too many collisions can hurt performance.

questions.prompt: A HashSet permits duplicate elements as distinct entries if their hash codes differ.
questions.explanation: Set models a collection with no duplicate elements according to its equality semantics; HashSet does not keep equal duplicates even when hash behavior is involved.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `ArrayList` is most accurate?

options.text: It is a resizable-array List with fast indexed access and typically costly middle insertions
It is a sorted tree with logarithmic indexed access
It is immutable after construction
It is a thread-safe queue by default

questions.explanation: ArrayList is a resizable-array implementation. Indexed get/set are constant-time, while insertions or removals away from the end may shift elements.

questions.prompt: Which interface is the standard abstraction for a double-ended queue?

options.text: Deque
Map
Set
Comparator

questions.explanation: Deque supports insertion and removal at both ends and can be used as a queue or stack abstraction.

questions.prompt: The Stream API stores its elements in a collection and can be traversed repeatedly without recreating the stream.
questions.explanation: A stream is a computation pipeline over a source, not a storage container. Streams are consumed by terminal operations and generally cannot be reused after consumption.

questions.prompt: Which operation is terminal in a Stream pipeline?

options.text: collect
map
filter
peek

questions.explanation: collect is a terminal operation that produces a result or side effect. map, filter, and peek are intermediate operations that build the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Stream intermediate operations are generally lazy and run when a terminal operation initiates traversal.
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations build a pipeline without processing elements immediately; traversal and evaluation are triggered by a terminal operation.

questions.prompt: What is a key risk when using `parallelStream()` with shared mutable state?

options.text: Unsynchronized updates can race and produce incorrect results
It guarantees a fixed encounter order for side effects
It automatically makes all objects immutable
It disables exception propagation

questions.explanation: Parallel execution may process elements concurrently. Behavioral parameters should avoid interference and unsafe shared mutable state; use reduction or collectors designed for parallelism.

questions.prompt: A Comparator can define an ordering independently of changing the compared class's natural ordering.
questions.explanation: Comparator is an external comparison strategy. It can be supplied to sorting APIs and ordered collections independently of the type's Comparable implementation.

questions.prompt: Which collection is designed to provide a priority queue ordered by natural order or a Comparator?

options.text: PriorityQueue
HashSet
ArrayList
IdentityHashMap

questions.explanation: PriorityQueue orders its head according to natural ordering or a Comparator; it does not promise that iteration traverses all elements in sorted order.

questions.prompt: HashMap iteration order is guaranteed to match insertion order.
questions.explanation: HashMap makes no guarantee of iteration order. LinkedHashMap is the usual choice when encounter order is required.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes `Optional<T>`?

options.text: A container that may or may not contain a non-null value, often used for a return value
A thread-safe replacement for every nullable field
A collection that always contains multiple values
A checked exception wrapper required for all methods

questions.explanation: Optional represents the presence or absence of a non-null value and is primarily intended as a method return type to express possible absence.

questions.prompt: The Stream API's `filter` operation changes the elements' values, while `map` only removes elements.
questions.explanation: filter selects elements matching a predicate; map transforms each element into a corresponding result.

questions.prompt: Which Map method computes a value only when a key is absent or mapped to null?

options.text: computeIfAbsent
replaceAll
containsValue
forEach

questions.explanation: Map.computeIfAbsent applies the mapping function when the specified key is absent or currently mapped to null, then associates a non-null result when returned.

questions.prompt: An unmodifiable collection view is necessarily a deep immutable copy of every object it exposes.
questions.explanation: Unmodifiable describes the collection's mutation interface; it does not necessarily make the backing collection independent or make the elements themselves immutable.

questions.prompt: What does `Collectors.groupingBy` primarily produce?

options.text: A Map grouping stream elements by a classification key
A sorted list of all input elements
A parallel thread pool
A filter that removes duplicates

questions.explanation: groupingBy is a collector that classifies elements by a key and accumulates values into groups, commonly a Map from key to list.

questions.prompt: What monitor does an instance synchronized method lock?

options.text: The monitor associated with `this`
The monitor associated with the class's Class object
A new private monitor for each invocation
No monitor; synchronized only affects compilation

questions.explanation: A synchronized instance method acquires the monitor associated with the receiver object. A static synchronized method uses the Class object monitor.

questions.prompt: What monitor does a static synchronized method use?

options.text: The Class object representing the declaring class
The `this` object of an arbitrary caller
A monitor shared with every class in the JVM
No monitor

questions.explanation: A static synchronized method synchronizes on the Class object associated with its declaring class, rather than an instance receiver.

questions.prompt: Entering and leaving a synchronized region can establish happens-before relationships between threads using the same monitor.
questions.explanation: Monitor unlock and subsequent lock actions on the same monitor participate in synchronization order and can establish happens-before visibility guarantees.

questions.prompt: What does `volatile` primarily guarantee for a field?

options.text: Visibility and ordering properties for reads/writes of that variable, not compound-operation atomicity
Atomicity of every sequence of operations using the field
Exclusive access to the containing object
Persistence of the field to disk

questions.explanation: Volatile reads and writes have memory-model visibility and ordering effects, but a compound action such as increment is not made atomic merely by declaring the variable volatile.

questions.prompt: The expression `volatileCounter++` is an atomic read-modify-write operation solely because the field is volatile.
questions.explanation: Increment consists of a read, arithmetic, and write; volatile does not combine those into one atomic operation. Use synchronization or an atomic class when atomicity is needed.

questions.prompt: What does `Thread.sleep` guarantee about synchronization locks held by the sleeping thread?

options.text: It does not release monitors the thread already holds
It releases every monitor until it wakes
It notifies all threads waiting on the current object
It transfers ownership of the lock to the caller

questions.explanation: Sleeping pauses a thread but does not release monitors it holds. Object.wait, unlike sleep, releases the monitor for the specified object while waiting.

questions.prompt: Calling `wait()` on an object requires owning that object's monitor.
questions.explanation: Object.wait requires the current thread to own the object's monitor; otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown. wait releases and later reacquires that monitor.

questions.prompt: Which API is generally preferred for managing groups of asynchronous tasks and lifecycle over manually creating many raw threads?

options.text: ExecutorService
System.gc
Object.finalize
StringBuilder

questions.explanation: ExecutorService separates task submission from thread management and provides lifecycle and result-handling APIs for managed execution.

questions.prompt: A Future can represent a result that may become available after a computation completes.
questions.explanation: Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation and offers operations to check completion, retrieve the result, or cancel the computation.

questions.prompt: What does an AtomicInteger provide for operations such as incrementAndGet?

options.text: Atomic update operations on an integer value without a separate explicit lock for each operation
Durable storage across process restarts
Automatic protection of unrelated fields
A guarantee that every update is wait-free in all circumstances

questions.explanation: AtomicInteger provides atomic operations on one integer value. It does not automatically coordinate invariants spanning other variables.

questions.prompt: An ExecutorService should be shut down when the application no longer needs it so it can stop accepting tasks and release resources.
questions.explanation: ExecutorService lifecycle methods support orderly shutdown or immediate cancellation attempts; callers should manage executor lifecycle rather than leave pools unmanaged.

questions.prompt: What does the happens-before relation express in the Java Memory Model?

options.text: A visibility and ordering guarantee between actions, not necessarily wall-clock chronology
The exact nanosecond time each thread runs
A guarantee that every thread executes serially
The order in which source files are compiled

questions.explanation: Happens-before is a partial-order relation used to determine whether actions are visible and ordered across threads. It is not a real-time scheduling guarantee.

questions.prompt: A data race occurs when conflicting accesses to a shared variable are not ordered by happens-before, with at least one access a write.
questions.explanation: The JMM's data-race concept involves conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before; races can make behavior surprising even if individual reads or writes seem simple.

questions.prompt: Which is the safer pattern for coordinating tasks that return values and may fail?

options.text: Submit Callable tasks to an ExecutorService and inspect their Futures
Start raw threads and assume exceptions return to the caller
Use Thread.sleep as a completion signal
Store all results in an unsynchronized static field

questions.explanation: Callable returns a value and can throw checked exceptions; Future provides completion/result access and reports task failures through its retrieval API.

questions.prompt: A final reference makes the referenced object deeply immutable automatically.
questions.explanation: final prevents reassignment of the reference variable after assignment, but does not prohibit mutation of the referenced object. Deep immutability requires immutable object state and reachable contents.

questions.prompt: In the Java module system, what does an `exports` directive primarily do?

options.text: Makes a package's public types accessible to other modules that read the exporting module
Adds a dependency on every module in the JDK
Opens a package only to reflection by all modules
Compiles the package into a native library

questions.explanation: A module exports packages as part of its accessible API. `opens` has a distinct role for reflective access, often at runtime.

questions.prompt: A package name and a module name are interchangeable concepts in Java's module system.
questions.explanation: Modules group packages and declare dependencies and exports; packages organize types. They are related but distinct names and structures.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a `requires` directive in `module-info.java`?

options.text: Declare a dependency on another named module
Export a package to all consumers
Mark a class as sealed
Configure a garbage collector

questions.explanation: A requires directive declares that one module depends on another module for compilation and resolution; modifiers can refine the dependency's semantics.

questions.prompt: The `java.base` module is a foundational module in the Java SE platform.
questions.explanation: The Java SE API specification describes java.base as defining foundational APIs and it is implicitly available to other modules.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `opens` versus `exports` is most accurate?

options.text: opens supports reflective access to package types; exports exposes public API access under module rules
They are exact synonyms
exports is only for reflection and opens is only for compilation
Neither directive affects access

questions.explanation: Exports controls ordinary access to public types in a package for reading modules; opens grants reflective access to types and members, typically for frameworks.

questions.prompt: How does a record's component list affect its generated API?

options.text: It declares the record's state components and corresponding component accessors
It declares a list of permitted subclasses
It creates mutable public fields by default
It is used only for serialization metadata

questions.explanation: Record components define the state description and correspond to component fields and accessor methods, along with other record members governed by the JLS.

questions.prompt: A default interface method has a method body and can be inherited by implementing classes unless overridden or otherwise conflicted.
questions.explanation: Default methods have an implementation body. Class and interface inheritance rules determine which implementation is inherited and when conflicts require resolution.

questions.prompt: What is heap pollution in the context of Java generics?

options.text: A variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized type
A garbage collector cannot reclaim an object
A generic class stores objects on the heap
An array is sorted incorrectly

questions.explanation: Heap pollution occurs when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized type, often due to unchecked operations or unsafe varargs interactions.

questions.prompt: A ConcurrentHashMap permits null keys and null values in its standard implementation contract.
questions.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap does not permit null keys or values; prohibiting null helps avoid ambiguity in concurrent retrieval and absence semantics.

questions.prompt: Which method can produce an immutable list snapshot from a collection in modern Java?

options.text: List.copyOf(collection)
collection.sort()
Arrays.asList(collection)
Collections.synchronizedList(collection)

questions.explanation: List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list containing the collection's elements as a snapshot; the contained objects themselves are not made deeply immutable.

questions.prompt: What happens if a `finally` block itself completes abruptly while another exception is propagating?

options.text: The abrupt completion of finally can replace the earlier completion reason
The original exception is always automatically restored
The finally block is ignored
Compilation always fails

questions.explanation: Under the JLS, if finally completes abruptly, its reason for abrupt completion is propagated and the prior reason can be discarded. This is one reason to avoid returning or throwing from finally casually.

questions.prompt: For floating-point comparisons, comparisons such as `<` and `>=` are both false when an operand is NaN.
questions.explanation: The JLS specifies that relational comparisons return false if either operand is NaN; this means common complementary comparisons are not logical complements in the presence of NaN.

questions.prompt: Which API best represents a sequence of values that may be absent or present as one value, rather than zero or many values?

options.text: Optional
Stream
Deque
Iterator

questions.explanation: Optional models a single possible value. Streams model pipelines over potentially many elements and collections store groups of values.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a local variable declared with `var` is correct?

options.text: Its type is inferred at compile time from its initializer; var does not make Java dynamically typed
Its type can change after assignment
It can be declared without an initializer in every context
It can be used for fields and method return types exactly like a universal type

questions.explanation: Local variable type inference determines a static compile-time type from the initializer; `var` is not a dynamic type and is restricted to permitted local variable declaration contexts.

questions.prompt: A stream pipeline's `count()` is a terminal operation, so the stream should not be reused afterward.
questions.explanation: count is a terminal operation. A stream is intended for one pipeline computation and should not be operated on again after a terminal operation has consumed it.

questions.prompt: Which Spring abstraction represents the IoC container responsible for creating, configuring, and assembling beans?

options.text: ApplicationContext
DispatcherServlet
JdbcTemplate
MockMvc

questions.explanation: Spring documents ApplicationContext as the IoC container interface responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling beans from configuration metadata.

questions.prompt: In Spring terminology, a bean is an object instantiated, assembled, and managed by the IoC container.
questions.explanation: A bean is an application object managed by the Spring container; dependencies and configuration metadata determine how it is constructed and assembled.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines dependency injection in Spring?

options.text: The container supplies an object's dependencies when it creates that object
A class searches globally for every dependency at runtime
The object compiles dependencies into its bytecode
The container removes all object references

questions.explanation: Dependency injection is a specialized form of IoC: objects expose dependencies through constructor arguments, factory-method arguments, or properties, and the container injects them during creation.

questions.prompt: Spring configuration metadata can be expressed using annotated components, Java configuration, XML, or supported script formats.
questions.explanation: The Spring reference describes configuration metadata as independent of format, including annotated component classes, configuration classes with factory methods, and external XML or Groovy scripts.

questions.prompt: What does a `@Bean`-annotated method in a Java `@Configuration` class typically declare?

options.text: A bean definition whose returned object is managed by the container
A database table
A request mapping
A test assertion

questions.explanation: Java-based Spring configuration commonly uses @Bean methods, each corresponding to a bean definition managed by the container.

questions.prompt: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit in the constructor signature.
questions.explanation: Constructor injection expresses dependencies through constructor arguments, making required collaborators visible when creating the object and supporting immutable fields where designed.

questions.prompt: If a Spring bean has exactly one constructor, what is generally true about constructor autowiring?

options.text: Spring can use that constructor without requiring `@Autowired` on it
The constructor is ignored unless it is private
All parameters must be optional
Spring requires XML configuration for the constructor

questions.explanation: Spring's annotation-based autowiring supports a single constructor as the injection constructor without needing @Autowired, subject to the applicable framework version and bean setup.

questions.prompt: `@Component` is a stereotype annotation that can make a class eligible for component scanning.
questions.explanation: @Component marks a class as a Spring-managed component; component scanning can detect it when its package is within the scan configuration.

questions.prompt: What does `@Primary` communicate when multiple beans match a single-valued dependency?

options.text: Prefer this bean as the primary candidate for autowiring
Create this bean before every other bean in all cases
Make the bean immutable
Exclude this bean from component scanning

questions.explanation: @Primary gives preference to a bean when multiple candidates are eligible for a single-valued injection point; qualifiers can select a specific candidate more explicitly.

questions.prompt: `@Qualifier` can narrow the candidates considered for an autowired dependency.
questions.explanation: Qualifier metadata narrows the set of candidate beans for a dependency; it is not simply a universal bean-name lookup mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which statement about singleton scope in Spring is most accurate?

options.text: It means one bean instance per bean definition per IoC container
It means exactly one instance across all JVMs and containers
It means one instance per HTTP request
It makes the bean thread-safe automatically

questions.explanation: Spring singleton scope is per bean definition per container, not the GoF singleton across a class loader or all application processes. Singleton scope does not itself guarantee thread safety.

questions.prompt: A prototype-scoped bean is created on each request from the container, and Spring does not manage its full destruction lifecycle in the same way as a singleton.
questions.explanation: Prototype scope creates a new instance for each container request. The container configures and returns it but does not track and invoke destruction callbacks for the prototype instance as it does for managed singletons.

questions.prompt: What problem can occur when a singleton bean directly holds a prototype bean injected only once?

options.text: The singleton retains the one prototype instance injected at its own creation rather than automatically receiving a new one per method call
The prototype becomes a singleton globally
Spring rejects all prototype dependencies
The singleton is recreated for every request

questions.explanation: A prototype dependency is resolved when the singleton is instantiated; ordinary field or constructor injection does not automatically perform a fresh lookup on every later use. Scoped proxies or providers can address this when required.

questions.prompt: The ApplicationContext supports internationalization messages and application events in addition to bean management.
questions.explanation: ApplicationContext extends basic bean-factory capabilities with features including message resource resolution and event publication/listening.

questions.prompt: What does `@Lazy` on a bean definition generally change?

options.text: Defers initialization of that bean until it is needed, subject to injection and other triggers
Makes every method asynchronous
Changes singleton scope into request scope
Prevents dependency injection

questions.explanation: Lazy initialization delays bean creation until requested; a lazy bean required by an eagerly initialized singleton may still be instantiated to satisfy that dependency unless a proxy/provider changes resolution timing.

questions.prompt: BeanFactory and ApplicationContext are identical interfaces with no additional capabilities in ApplicationContext.
questions.explanation: ApplicationContext builds on BeanFactory and adds broader application-level capabilities, such as events and message resolution, alongside integrated context support.

questions.prompt: Which option is generally preferred over calling `ApplicationContext.getBean()` throughout business code?

options.text: Declare dependencies and let the container inject them
Use a global static context in every class
Create a new context for each method call
Store dependencies in system properties

questions.explanation: Spring recommends that application code generally avoid direct service-locator calls to getBean and instead express dependencies for injection, reducing coupling to Spring APIs.

questions.prompt: Spring can assemble dependencies using constructor arguments, factory-method arguments, or properties, depending on configuration.
questions.explanation: Spring DI supports dependencies supplied through constructor arguments, factory method arguments, and properties set after instantiation.

questions.prompt: What does `@Profile(
)` on a component or configuration class express?

options.text: Register it only when the `dev` profile is active
Register it only when the JVM uses a development vendor
Set the logging level to DEBUG automatically
Make all injected dependencies optional

questions.explanation: @Profile limits component, configuration, or configuration-properties registration to environments where the specified profile expression matches.

questions.prompt: Spring's `@DependsOn` declares an explicit initialization dependency between named beans; it is not the usual way to inject a collaborator reference.
questions.explanation: @DependsOn expresses initialization ordering for beans; actual collaborators should normally be expressed as injected dependencies.

questions.prompt: What is the central purpose of Spring AOP in typical proxy-based use?

options.text: Apply cross-cutting behavior such as advice around matched method executions
Replace Java's type system
Persist every bean automatically
Compile every class into a database schema

questions.explanation: Spring AOP modularizes cross-cutting concerns using aspects, pointcuts, and advice, commonly through proxies around Spring-managed objects.

questions.prompt: In proxy-based Spring AOP, a self-invocation through `this` normally bypasses the proxy and therefore does not trigger proxy advice on the called method.
questions.explanation: Proxy-based advice applies to calls entering through the proxy. A method calling another method on the same target via this does not re-enter the proxy, so the second call is not advised in the usual proxy mode.

questions.prompt: Which AOP term selects the join points at which advice should run?

options.text: Pointcut
Bean scope
Application event
Property source

questions.explanation: A pointcut is a predicate that matches join points; advice defines the action to execute at matched join points.

questions.prompt: An `@AfterReturning` advice runs only when the advised method returns normally.
questions.explanation: After-returning advice runs after a matched method invocation completes normally; exceptional completion is handled by other advice types such as after-throwing or after-finally.

questions.prompt: What does `@Around` advice allow an aspect to do?

options.text: Control whether and when the intercepted invocation proceeds, and inspect its result or exception
Only observe bean construction without affecting method calls
Declare a database foreign key
Activate a profile

questions.explanation: Around advice receives a ProceedingJoinPoint and can call proceed, possibly with altered arguments, and control behavior before and after the target invocation.

questions.prompt: Spring application events are always delivered asynchronously by default.
questions.explanation: The default event multicaster is synchronous unless configured otherwise, so a listener usually runs in the publisher's thread by default.

questions.prompt: Which Spring abstraction publishes an application event to the context?

options.text: ApplicationEventPublisher
BeanDefinitionReader
HandlerMethodArgumentResolver
TransactionStatus

questions.explanation: ApplicationEventPublisher is the event-publishing abstraction; listeners can receive matching events through supported listener mechanisms such as @EventListener.

questions.prompt: `@Transactional` commonly relies on Spring AOP proxies in its default proxy mode, so self-invocation can bypass transaction advice.
questions.explanation: Declarative transaction annotations are commonly applied through proxies. Calls that do not cross the proxy boundary, such as a self-invocation, do not receive proxy-based transaction interception.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an AOP advice type `@Before`?

options.text: It runs before the matched method execution and cannot itself replace the method's return value
It runs only after successful return
It always suppresses the target method
It runs once at application startup

questions.explanation: Before advice executes before the join point. It can affect whether invocation continues by throwing an exception, but it does not proceed-and-return a replacement result like around advice.

questions.prompt: Spring AOP proxy advice automatically intercepts every private method call on a target object in proxy mode.
questions.explanation: Proxy-based Spring AOP intercepts calls through proxies to eligible methods; private methods and internal self-invocations are not intercepted in the same way as externally invoked proxy methods.

questions.prompt: What does Spring Boot auto-configuration use as an important input when proposing configuration?

options.text: The jar dependencies present on the classpath, along with conditions and existing beans
Only the name of the main class
The source-control branch name
Only the operating system time zone

questions.explanation: Spring Boot attempts configuration based on added jar dependencies and conditional criteria; existing user-defined beans can cause default configuration to back away.

questions.prompt: A typical Spring Boot application opts into auto-configuration through `@EnableAutoConfiguration` or `@SpringBootApplication`.
questions.explanation: The reference documents either annotation as an opt-in mechanism; @SpringBootApplication includes the enable-auto-configuration capability.

questions.prompt: If a user defines their own DataSource bean, what may happen to embedded-database auto-configuration?

options.text: The default embedded database configuration backs away when the user configuration replaces it
Spring Boot always creates a second DataSource
The application context is forcibly disabled
The bean is ignored because auto-configuration always wins

questions.explanation: Auto-configuration is designed to be non-invasive. For example, when the user defines a DataSource, relevant default embedded database support backs away.

questions.prompt: The `--debug` switch can help reveal which auto-configuration conditions matched or did not match through a conditions report.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot documents starting with --debug to enable condition evaluation reporting, helping explain applied auto-configuration.

questions.prompt: Which annotation attribute can exclude an unwanted auto-configuration class when its type is available?

options.text: `exclude` on `@SpringBootApplication` or `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
`value` on `@Component`
`profile` on `@Bean`
`throws` on the main method

questions.explanation: The auto-configuration annotation supports exclusion by class, and excludeName supports exclusion by fully qualified name when the class is not on the classpath.

questions.prompt: Spring Boot recommends placing multiple `@SpringBootApplication` annotations across the application as a normal way to enable auto-configuration repeatedly.
questions.explanation: The reference recommends one @SpringBootApplication or @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation, generally on the primary configuration class.

questions.prompt: What is the typical role of a Spring Boot starter?

options.text: Provide a convenient dependency descriptor for a common application capability
Replace the Java compiler
Store runtime passwords in source code
Generate a database backup automatically

questions.explanation: Starters simplify dependency setup by grouping common dependencies; auto-configuration may then configure supported capabilities when those dependencies and conditions are present.

questions.prompt: A user-defined bean can replace or cause conditional auto-configuration for a corresponding default to back off.
questions.explanation: Many auto-configurations are conditional and back off when an application supplies its own matching bean, allowing gradual customization.

questions.prompt: What is the default package area commonly used by auto-configured features to find entities and repositories?

options.text: The auto-configuration package derived from the application configuration location
Every package in every dependency jar
Only `java.lang`
The current working directory's folder name

questions.explanation: The package of the configuration class carrying @EnableAutoConfiguration, directly or via @SpringBootApplication, establishes the default auto-configuration package used by features scanning for entities and repositories.

questions.prompt: Spring Boot auto-configuration is intended to be non-invasive and can be selectively excluded.
questions.explanation: Defaults can back away in response to user configuration and specific auto-configuration classes can be excluded by annotation or property.

questions.prompt: What does `@SpringBootApplication` combine at a high level?

options.text: Boot configuration, component scanning, and auto-configuration enablement
JPA, security, and actuator unconditionally
A test runner and database migration tool
Only a request mapping

questions.explanation: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation that combines configuration, component scanning, and auto-configuration enablement; it does not unconditionally add every technology integration.

questions.prompt: A class annotated with `@SpringBootApplication` is generally used as a primary source for bootstrapping the application context.
questions.explanation: The main application class is commonly the primary configuration source passed to SpringApplication, and the annotation provides the application configuration conventions.

questions.prompt: How does component scanning find a class annotated with `@Service` in a conventional Boot application?

options.text: It scans the package of the application configuration and its subpackages by default
It scans only the Java standard library
It requires a database query
It scans all packages on the machine

questions.explanation: Component scanning starts from the package containing the scan configuration and scans its subpackages; placing the main application class in a suitable root package is a common convention.

questions.prompt: `@Repository`, `@Service`, and `@Controller` are specialized component stereotypes associated with different application roles.
questions.explanation: These annotations specialize the general component stereotype semantically; component scanning can detect them, and some stereotypes enable additional framework behavior.

questions.prompt: Which injection style most clearly exposes mandatory dependencies and supports a fully initialized object?

options.text: Constructor injection
Looking up dependencies in a static global map
Setting undocumented fields by reflection in business code
Reading dependency class names from standard input

questions.explanation: Constructor injection declares required collaborators in the constructor and allows the object to be built in a valid state; it also supports final fields.

questions.prompt: A Spring singleton bean is inherently thread-safe because only one instance exists per container.
questions.explanation: Singleton means one instance per bean definition per container, not automatic thread safety. Concurrent requests can call the same singleton instance; mutable shared state still needs safe design.

questions.prompt: What does `@Qualifier(
)` typically do at an injection point?

options.text: Narrows candidates using qualifier metadata so the intended compatible bean can be selected
Changes the bean to prototype scope
Starts the bean asynchronously
Marks the injection as optional without affecting selection

questions.explanation: Qualifier values help distinguish among multiple type-compatible candidates. They are candidate-selection metadata and need not be identical to a bean name in every use.

questions.prompt: The default Spring bean scope is singleton.
questions.explanation: Spring's default bean scope is singleton: one shared instance per bean definition per container.

questions.prompt: What is a practical risk of injecting a prototype bean into a singleton using ordinary constructor injection?

options.text: The prototype is resolved once while creating the singleton, not once per later use
The singleton is converted into prototype scope
The prototype can never be instantiated
The container creates one prototype per JVM forever

questions.explanation: The singleton's dependency is resolved at singleton creation time. Use a provider or scoped proxy if the singleton needs a fresh prototype instance for each operation.

questions.prompt: `@Lazy` on an injection point can defer resolution of a dependency through a lazy-resolution proxy in supported Spring configuration.
questions.explanation: Spring supports lazy-resolution proxies for dependencies marked lazy at injection points; calls resolve the target when needed, subject to proxy semantics.

questions.prompt: Which set lists supported Spring Boot external configuration sources?

options.text: Properties/YAML files, environment variables, and command-line arguments
Only XML files packaged in the jar
Only Java constants compiled into classes
Only values returned by a database

questions.explanation: Spring Boot supports externalized configuration from sources including properties and YAML, environment variables, command-line arguments, JSON properties, and more.

questions.prompt: `@ConfigurationProperties` can bind external properties into structured objects.
questions.explanation: ConfigurationProperties binds related external configuration keys to a structured Java object, while @Value targets individual values and Environment provides programmatic access.

questions.prompt: Which property source has higher precedence in the documented common Spring Boot ordering: command-line arguments or packaged `application.properties`?

options.text: Command-line arguments
Packaged application.properties
They always have identical precedence
Neither is added to the Environment

questions.explanation: Spring Boot's external configuration ordering places command-line properties later than packaged config data, so command-line values can override packaged defaults.

questions.prompt: An `application-prod.properties` file is a conventional profile-specific configuration file for the `prod` profile.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot loads profile-specific config files using the application-{profile} naming convention, such as application-prod.properties or YAML variants, when that profile is active.

questions.prompt: How can the `prod` profile commonly be activated from a command line?

options.text: `--spring.profiles.active=prod`
`--profile=prod`
`--spring.active.profile=prod`
`-Dspring.profile=prod` only

questions.explanation: Spring Boot allows spring.profiles.active to be set as a property, including as the command-line option --spring.profiles.active=prod.

questions.prompt: `@Profile` can conditionally register components, configuration classes, or configuration-properties types based on active profiles.
questions.explanation: The profiles documentation describes @Profile on components, configuration classes, and configuration-properties classes to restrict registration by profile expression.

questions.prompt: What is the practical value of externalized configuration?

options.text: Use the same application code with different environment-specific settings
Avoid compiling Java source code
Guarantee every property is secret
Remove the need for configuration validation

questions.explanation: Externalized configuration separates settings from application code so the same artifact can be configured differently across environments. Sensitive values still require appropriate secret management.

questions.prompt: Profile-specific configuration files always override every possible higher-precedence source, including command-line options.
questions.explanation: Profile-specific files participate in an ordered property-source system; higher-precedence sources such as command-line properties can override them.

questions.prompt: Which Spring abstraction provides programmatic access to resolved configuration properties?

options.text: Environment
ApplicationRunner only
BeanFactoryPostProcessor only
DispatcherServlet

questions.explanation: Spring's Environment abstraction provides programmatic property access and profile information, alongside binding mechanisms such as @ConfigurationProperties.

questions.prompt: Spring Boot converts command-line arguments such as `--server.port=9000` into properties in the Environment by default.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot documents that SpringApplication converts command-line option arguments beginning with -- into properties and adds them to the Environment by default.

questions.prompt: In Spring MVC, which central servlet commonly dispatches incoming HTTP requests to controllers and other web components?

options.text: DispatcherServlet
ContextLoaderListener
JdbcTemplate
TaskScheduler

questions.explanation: DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller; it coordinates request mapping, handler execution, and response processing.

questions.prompt: `@RestController` combines controller semantics with response-body serialization for handler methods by default.
questions.explanation: RestController is a composed annotation combining Controller and ResponseBody, so handler return values are written to the response body through appropriate message converters.

questions.prompt: What does `@GetMapping(
)` principally declare?

options.text: A handler mapping for HTTP GET requests matching the path pattern
A database table named items
A bean scope
A scheduled task

questions.explanation: GetMapping is a composed request-mapping annotation for HTTP GET; path variables can bind matching path segments to handler parameters.

questions.prompt: `@PathVariable` binds a handler method parameter from a URI template variable such as `{id}`.
questions.explanation: PathVariable resolves a parameter from a named URI template variable in the matched request mapping.

questions.prompt: Which annotation commonly binds a JSON request body to a Java method argument using an HTTP message converter?

options.text: @RequestBody
@PathVariable
@RequestHeader only
@Profile

questions.explanation: RequestBody reads the request body and converts it to the declared argument type through an HttpMessageConverter; validation can be applied with supported validation annotations.

questions.prompt: `@RequestParam` can bind query parameters or form data to a controller method parameter.
questions.explanation: RequestParam binds request parameters, including query parameters and form data in applicable MVC contexts, with configurable required and default-value behavior.

questions.prompt: What is the role of an HttpMessageConverter in Spring MVC?

options.text: Read and write HTTP request/response bodies for Java types
Choose database transaction isolation
Register application profiles
Create thread pools for every controller

questions.explanation: HttpMessageConverter implementations convert between HTTP bodies and Java objects, supporting formats such as JSON when suitable converters are present.

questions.prompt: Returning `ResponseEntity<T>` can let a controller specify the response status and headers as well as the body.
questions.explanation: ResponseEntity represents an HTTP response, including status, headers, and an optional body.

questions.prompt: Which annotation is commonly used to centralize exception handling across multiple controllers?

options.text: @ControllerAdvice
@Bean
@Primary
@EnableScheduling

questions.explanation: ControllerAdvice applies shared controller advice, including exception handlers, across controllers; RestControllerAdvice adds response-body semantics.

questions.prompt: Spring MVC validation can be integrated with request binding when a supported validation provider is present.
questions.explanation: Spring MVC supports validation for bound request objects when validation infrastructure is available and applicable validation annotations are used; exact behavior depends on method signature and framework version.

questions.prompt: What does Spring's `@Transactional` primarily express?

options.text: A method or class should participate in transaction behavior managed by Spring's transaction infrastructure
The method must execute on a new operating-system process
The method is automatically idempotent
Every exception is always rolled back

questions.explanation: Transactional metadata configures declarative transaction behavior through a transaction manager/interceptor; rollback rules and propagation/isolation settings determine details.

questions.prompt: In Spring's default declarative transaction settings, unchecked exceptions typically trigger rollback, while checked exceptions do not by default.
questions.explanation: The conventional default rollback rules roll back on RuntimeException and Error, not checked exceptions, unless rollback rules are customized. Confirm exact version-specific configuration when using newer global defaults.

questions.prompt: What does transaction propagation `REQUIRED` generally mean?

options.text: Join an existing transaction or create one if none exists
Always suspend every existing transaction and create a new one
Never use a transaction
Retry the method until it succeeds

questions.explanation: REQUIRED is the common propagation behavior: participate in the current transaction if present, otherwise start a new transaction.

questions.prompt: In proxy mode, calling a transactional method from another method on the same object usually crosses the Spring proxy boundary.
questions.explanation: A same-object self-invocation uses the target's this reference and bypasses the proxy, so proxy-based transactional advice is not applied to that internal call.

questions.prompt: Which Spring abstraction centralizes JDBC resource handling and reduces repetitive JDBC boilerplate?

options.text: JdbcTemplate
DispatcherServlet
ApplicationEventPublisher
MockMvc

questions.explanation: JdbcTemplate manages common JDBC workflow such as resource acquisition/release and exception translation while application code supplies SQL and row mapping.

questions.prompt: Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy is designed to provide a consistent exception abstraction across supported data-access technologies.
questions.explanation: Spring translates technology-specific persistence exceptions into its data-access exception hierarchy, providing a consistent unchecked abstraction.

questions.prompt: What does Spring Data's `CrudRepository` provide at a high level?

options.text: A repository abstraction for common create, read, update, and delete operations
An HTTP request dispatcher
A transaction manager implementation for every datastore
A Java compiler plugin

questions.explanation: CrudRepository exposes common repository operations; concrete Spring Data modules provide datastore-specific repository implementations and semantics.

questions.prompt: A Spring Data repository interface can often be implemented at runtime by repository infrastructure when enabled and correctly configured.
questions.explanation: Spring Data repository infrastructure creates proxy implementations for repository interfaces based on the selected store module and configuration.

questions.prompt: Which annotation commonly maps a JPA entity type?

options.text: @Entity
@RestController
@ConfigurationProperties
@EventListener

questions.explanation: Jakarta Persistence @Entity marks a class as a persistent entity. Spring Boot's JPA integration can configure supporting infrastructure when dependencies and conditions are satisfied.

questions.prompt: A database transaction automatically includes a remote HTTP call in the same local JDBC transaction.
questions.explanation: A local database transaction does not automatically make a separate remote HTTP operation atomic with the database. Distributed consistency requires an explicit design such as outbox, saga, or supported distributed transaction coordination.

questions.prompt: What does `@SpringBootTest` primarily do in a test?

options.text: Create an ApplicationContext using Spring Boot's test bootstrap support
Run only a plain Java unit test without a context
Mock every dependency automatically
Build and publish a production image

questions.explanation: SpringBootTest loads an application context using Spring Boot's test support; it is broader than a plain unit test and can be configured with web environment options.

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot test can often locate its primary configuration by searching upward from the package containing the test.
questions.explanation: When not specified, Boot test annotations search upward from the test package for a primary configuration such as @SpringBootApplication or @SpringBootConfiguration.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a test slice such as `@WebMvcTest`?

options.text: Load a focused subset of application configuration for testing a particular layer
Always start every production service and database
Replace assertions with logging
Run only Java compilation

questions.explanation: Spring Boot test slices load a focused set of auto-configurations and components for a layer, reducing the scope compared with a full application context.

questions.prompt: `@WebMvcTest` is generally intended to focus on Spring MVC components rather than load the entire application's persistence layer by default.
questions.explanation: WebMvcTest is a test slice for MVC infrastructure and controllers; dependencies outside the slice are commonly supplied as mocks or imported explicitly.

questions.prompt: Which Spring test utility can perform requests against MVC controllers without starting a real HTTP server?

options.text: MockMvc
JdbcTemplate
ApplicationRunner
BeanWrapper

questions.explanation: MockMvc exercises Spring MVC request handling using mock servlet infrastructure without requiring a live server socket.

questions.prompt: A test annotated `@Transactional` may have test-managed transaction behavior that rolls back after the test, depending on the test framework setup.
questions.explanation: Spring TestContext supports test-managed transactions; transactional tests are typically rolled back by default unless configured otherwise or explicitly committed.

questions.prompt: What is `@TestConfiguration` commonly used for in a Spring Boot test?

options.text: Declare additional or customized test-only configuration
Activate production auto-configuration exclusions globally
Map an HTTP endpoint
Create a database migration automatically

questions.explanation: A nested or imported TestConfiguration can customize a test's primary configuration or contribute test-specific beans without being treated as ordinary production configuration in the same way.

questions.prompt: `@RestClientTest` can configure support for testing REST clients, including a mock server facility in supported setups.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot's RestClientTest slice focuses on REST client components and can auto-configure client builders and MockRestServiceServer support depending on the configured client technology.

questions.prompt: Why are focused slice tests often faster and more diagnostic than loading the entire context for every test?

options.text: They load fewer components and auto-configurations for the layer under test
They skip all application assertions
They guarantee no mocks are needed
They execute tests on a different language runtime

questions.explanation: A slice narrows context setup to a particular area, which can improve speed and make failures more localized; it does not eliminate the need for appropriate test doubles or assertions.

questions.prompt: `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` can start an embedded server on a randomly selected port for integration testing.
questions.explanation: SpringBootTest supports web environment modes including RANDOM_PORT, which starts a server on an available random port for end-to-end HTTP tests.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Spring Boot Actuator?

options.text: Provide production-oriented monitoring and management features
Replace Spring's IoC container
Generate Java language specifications
Create UI layouts for React Native

questions.explanation: Actuator adds production-ready capabilities for monitoring and managing applications, including health, metrics, and management endpoints.

questions.prompt: Actuator endpoints can be exposed through HTTP or JMX, subject to configuration and security controls.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot supports managing and monitoring through HTTP endpoints or JMX. Exposure and access should be deliberately configured, especially in production.

questions.prompt: Which Actuator endpoint is conventionally used to report application health?

options.text: health
beansOnly
compile
dependencies

questions.explanation: The health endpoint provides health information and can include contributors for components such as databases, depending on configuration and access policy.

questions.prompt: Every Actuator endpoint is necessarily exposed over HTTP to every unauthenticated caller by default in production.
questions.explanation: Endpoint availability, exposure, and authorization are configurable; sensitive management endpoints should be limited and secured rather than assumed publicly exposed.

questions.prompt: What is Micrometer's typical role in a Spring Boot application?

options.text: Provide an instrumentation facade for application metrics and monitoring systems
Serve as the HTTP router
Replace Java's garbage collector
Provide the transaction rollback rules

questions.explanation: Micrometer is an application metrics facade integrated with Boot's observability and Actuator support, allowing instrumentation to be exported to supported monitoring systems.

questions.prompt: Spring Boot's externalized logging settings can be used independently of the underlying logging implementation for common configuration properties.
questions.explanation: Spring Boot provides logging properties that are independent of the selected logging infrastructure for common settings, while implementation-specific features may use implementation-specific configuration.

questions.prompt: What can `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON` provide to a Spring Boot application?

options.text: Inline JSON properties that are parsed into the Spring Environment
A compiled Java class file
A replacement for all bean definitions
A database schema migration

questions.explanation: Spring Boot can parse JSON embedded in the SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON environment variable or corresponding system property and add its properties to the Environment.

questions.prompt: A `@RequestBody` argument is typically populated from the HTTP request body using a suitable message converter.
questions.explanation: Spring MVC delegates request body conversion to configured HttpMessageConverter implementations, such as JSON converters when present.

questions.prompt: Which transaction propagation mode explicitly requests a new transaction while suspending an existing one when supported?

options.text: REQUIRES_NEW
REQUIRED
SUPPORTS
NEVER

questions.explanation: REQUIRES_NEW always uses an independent transaction; an existing transaction is suspended while the new one runs, subject to transaction-manager support.

questions.prompt: A profile expression can combine profile names with operators such as `&`, `|`, and `!` where supported.
questions.explanation: Spring profile expressions support logical combinations, such as AND, OR, and negation; expressions should use valid syntax and avoid mixing AND and OR without grouping where required.
